extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters and fiction writers (writers seeking to create emotionally truthful, dramatically structured scenes and stories)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating dramatic scenes and overall story substance for cinema and other narrative fiction, emphasizing conflict, the 'gap' between expectation and result, escalating risk, and writing from the character's interior. Practical techniques for scene design, point-of-view work, and avoiding cliché/exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude life's minutiae; create moments of antagonism
rubrics_metrics.description: Never include the ordinary minutiae of life in a story; instead concentrate on the moment in which a character takes an action expecting a useful reaction but instead provokes forces of antagonism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McKee emphasizes: 'BUT NEVER, EVER IN A STORY.' The writer should cut the everyday enabling reactions (the driver braking, the person answering the phone helpfully) and focus only on those instants where the world's reaction is different or stronger than expected, because those are what make life interesting on the page or screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three levels of conflict (concentric circles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's world comprises concentric circles of antagonism: (1) the inner circle — conflicts within self (mind, body, emotion); (2) personal relationships — intimacy beyond social role (family, lovers, friends); (3) extra-personal conflict — outside sources (institutions, other individuals, natural and man-made environments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three levels to locate and vary sources of antagonism. Examples: inner failures of mind or body; parent/child or lover/lover relationship conflicts that go deeper than role; conflicts with government, corporation, cops/criminals, time, space, and objects. Each level offers different dramatic possibilities and can be combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Gap — where subjective expectation meets objective necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is born where the subjective and objective realms touch: the protagonist acts expecting a probable reaction, but the objective world reacts differently or more powerfully, opening a gap between anticipation and result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish probability (what the character expects) from necessity (what actually happens). The gap between them is the nexus of story; it forces the character to reassess and take new, riskier actions. Build scenes so an action's anticipated result is displaced by an unexpected, necessary outcome that generates conflict and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure desire by risk; ask 'What is the risk?'
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a character's desire is directly proportional to the risk he or she is willing to take; to test any story ask: 'What is the risk? What does the protagonist stand to lose if he does not get what he wants? What’s the worst thing that will happen?','guidance':'If the worst outcome is merely a return to normal, the story is misconceived and uninteresting. High-value desires require high stakes (time, money, people, freedom, life, soul). Use concrete, compelling risks to justify pursuit and sustain audience investment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the worst outcome is merely a return to normal, the story is misconceived and uninteresting. High-value desires require high stakes (time, money, people, freedom, life, soul). Use concrete, compelling risks to justify pursuit and sustain audience investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive gap / escalating stakes (gap in progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: A protagonist's first action provokes antagonism and opens a gap; the protagonist adapts, takes a more difficult action, which again provokes antagonism and opens a larger gap — this progression repeats with increasingly risky actions until a final action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sequences so each beat forces a reassessment and escalation: each new action should require more willpower, capacity, and risk. This progressive 'upping of the ante' creates momentum and culminates in a final action that resolves (or tragically denies) the desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: True action vs mere activity
rubrics_metrics.description: True action is physical, vocal, or mental movement that opens gaps in expectation and creates significant change; mere activity is behavior where expected results happen and produce no meaningful change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize scenes and beats that rupture expectation and change the character's situation or perception. Cull scenes that are only activity (expected outcomes, trivial change), as they waste time and dilute dramatic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from the inside out; use Stanislavski’s 'Magic if'
rubrics_metrics.description: To create emotional truth, the writer must inhabit the character's center of awareness: ask 'If I were this character in these circumstances, what would I do?' and act that role imaginatively to generate honest, character-specific emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid distant questions ('How should someone take this action?' or 'If my character were in these circumstances, what would he do?' asked at a remove) because they produce clichés or 'cute' cleverness. Instead, use the writer's own emotional memory and improvisation (inner acting) to produce specific, believable reactions. Many great playwrights/screenwriters were also actors; adopt that improvisational, performative mindset at the desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inner monologues and ultra-slow rehearsal to find beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Write inner monologues to put a scene into 'ultra-slow motion' — words for flights of feeling or flashes of insight — even if minutes on screen take days to write on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put each moment under a microscope: rehearse the scene in the character’s mind, create chains of unspoken thoughts, images, sensations and emotions. This detailed internal work yields emotionally truthful actions and dialogue that will move an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift point of view among characters (and objects) to pry open gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: After creating an honest moment from one POV, move around the story universe—into other characters’ minds or even inanimate perspectives—to imagine reactions that will be unexpected from the first POV and thus splinter open the gap between expectation and result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method: settle into one character and ask 'If I were this character…' to create a beat; then 'step out' and ask the opposite POV question in another character. Repeat iteratively, returning to the first character with the new circumstances to discover new reactions. This POV-hopping is how to find oppositions and contradictions that deepen drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek opposites; use dialectical thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should doubt appearances and seek the opposite of the obvious; creative energy comes from contradiction and the breakthrough of appearances toward an unknown reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'What is the opposite of that?' to generate unexpected reactions and truths. Use dialectical play—contradiction and counterpoint—to reveal the hidden, inappropriate, or deeper truth within a scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize reactions over events
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine writing focuses less on what happens and more on to whom it happens, why, and how; the richest pleasures come from the reactions events cause and the insight gained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when plot points are conventional by genre (lovers meet, detective finds a crime), the dramatic interest comes from the specificity of who reacts and the psychological and emotional consequences. Shape scenes to reveal character through response rather than merely advancing plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define scene objectives for characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Every character in a scene should have a clear scene objective (what they want in that scene) which drives their actions and choices (e.g., Gittes’ scene objective: to find the truth; Evelyn’s scene objective: to hide her secret and escape with Katherine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and write each character’s objective before drafting a scene. Use those objectives to create conflict when characters' objectives clash, and to shape beats, choices, and escalation within the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive explanatory exposition; prefer concise revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthy expository explanation that slows pace can weaken character and antagonist; instead favor concise revelations that sustain dramatic power (example: cutting a long Evelyn exposition in CHINATOWN and replacing it with the terse exchange 'He raped you?' preserved antagonist's cruelty and the scene's power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for rewrites where exposition explains too much and flattens stakes or sympathy. Use implication, compressed beats, and pointed dialogue to reveal crucial backstory at high dramatic value and pace.
